messages.subject: wordcount of a big file
messages.body_plain:
I have a cluster with 3 servers, running Hadoop 2.0.0-cdh4.3.0, R version 3.0.1 and rmr 2.2.2
I'm using wordcount as a performance test.
When I use a big text file (around 3GB), while "reduce" task I've seen that R is getting a lot of memory and also that there's only one reduce task.

I wonder why I only have only one reduce task and why R gets so much memory. What can I do to increase the number of reducers and/or decrease the memory used by R?

Test file has 100.000.000 lines, each one has a line number followed by 5 random rumbers between 0 and 32000.

wordcount =
  function(
    input,
    output = NULL,
    pattern = " "){

wc.map =
      function(., lines) {
        keyval(
          unlist(
            strsplit(
              x = lines,
              split = pattern)),
          1)}

wc.reduce =
      function(word, counts ) {
        keyval(word, sum(counts))}

mapreduce(
      input = input,
      input.format = "text",
      output = output,
      map = wc.map,
      reduce = wc.reduce,
      combine = T)
}

messages.subject: Re: wordcount of a big file
messages.body_plain:
First keep in mind examples are in general not optimizes but kept as simple as possible.

The number of reduce tasks defaults to one in many Hadoop distribution. You need to change that. One way is to supply this additional argument to mapreduce

backend.parameters = list(hadoop= list(D = "mapred.reduce.tasks=10"))

where 10 should be actually slightly less than the number of available reduce slots. This argument is deprecated because it was being abused, but I think this use case will be preserved by whatever replaces it. The memory issue points to something else, like a word with a very large count. Even then, with the combiner on, it should work. Nonetheless I would check that the pattern is appropriate for your file, that would be single space separated words. Another thing is to try with a smaller, local file, say 1 mb, on the local backend, do a debug(wc.map) and debug(wc.reduce) and see that it is doing what you expect it to do. Have you tried different data sizes and wrote down the different times-to-completion for the map phase and reduce pahse? How do they grow? That usually gives some insight.  Another thing you can do is adding

rmr.str(word)
rmr.str(counts)

as the first two lines of the reduce function. It will write a lot in your std error, so use at smaller data sizes.
This is just an example after all and it hasn't been tested on more than one file. Pretty much the debugging guideline on the wiki can be used a little bit also a performance troubleshooting guide. There are other things you can try to do to move the work to the map phase, but I would first understand what the problem is instead of trying solutions. My suspicion is that your lines are short, vocabulary huge and uniformly distributed. In real life lines are longer, vocabulary smaller and with a zipf distribution. That could explain speed issues but not memory issues, so we need to dig deeper to figure out what's wrong.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#999] RHadoop : Using custom input format
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
off the bat the only problem I see here is the mode, which should be "text". I am not sure if that's going to make a huge difference, particularly on unix-like systems, but you are in uncharted territory, since the csv format uses a text connection. As far as your expectations, they are wrong, what you should get out of from.csv is a list of two elements, one NULL an one a data frame, the concatenation of the data frames returned by my.reader as second arg to keyval. What you are actually seeing defies both your and my expectations. Since you are just using from.dfs and not calling mapreduce, this should be relatively easy to debug. Unfortunately, for some reason debug(my.input.format$format) doesn't work. That's something for the R core members to fix so let's talk about workarounds. Modify my.reader with a browser() call. Try to read again. Inspect what you are getting from the connection (just do a  readLine and then start over again, as that will invalidate the rest of the parsing).  my.reader needs to return
keyval(NULL, list(df))
or the data frames will be rbinded. Let me know what you find and I'll try to help. I hope your files are relatively small, otherwise the whole strategy is doomed. Maybe in the low GB it is still going to work. I would keep some system monitoring constantly on because you are pushing a little bit in the opposite direction of what the design was, which is read x records at a time, process, move on.

Antonio

Sorry if I am not very clear with my question. I dont have access to my source code right now. I will share the code soon.

Meanwhile, I am trying to understand your comments.

"You wrote myformat so you can change it as you please, right? Then change the last line to the above expression, and you are good to go. Now from.dfs will be concatenating lists instead of rbinding data frames. "

Since I use "read.table" to read the "con" in "my.reader", it just returns one big data frame consisting all the rows in my 5 CSV files. But I what need is "keyval(NULL, list(df)) " where each data frame in the list contains rows of one CSV file. So if I have 100 CSV files, this list should contain 100 data frames. Since this does not work, I think either make.input.format is not able to use my "WholeFileInputFormat.java" or it is ignoring it because of some programming errors. Is there any way to debug this? If I add any print statements in "WholeFileInputFormat.java", would it show up in some logs. When I run map reduce jobs, I have seen these logs showing up in job specific stdout files. I am not sure whether "from.dfs" would also store them somewhere.

On Hadoop end,  I have jarred "WholeFileInputFormat.java" and "WholeFileRecordReader.java" and placed it in <HADOOP_HOME>/lib folder. In my java version of map reduce, I set my file format in JobConf. Now each mapper emits byte array of just one file. In reducer, I read the byte array into byte array input stream and fetch my column values and call some custom functions and emit the results in sequence file. This works perfectly fine.

If I have not explained it clearly yet, I will share the code Monday so that it might be easier to understand what I need.

Appreciate your responses.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm stuck with using equijoin and hoping to get help here. I have the following code:

bigmatrix1=matrix(rexp(4000, rate=.1), ncol=4)
bigmatrix1=cbind(1:1000,bigmatrix1)
bigmatrix2=matrix(rexp(4000, rate=.1), ncol=4)
bigmatrix2=cbind(1:1000,bigmatrix2)

map_test=    function(key, number_matrix){
         keys=number_matrix[,1]
         vals=number_matrix[,2:3]
       keyval(keys, vals)
     }

test1 =
  mapreduce (
  input = to.dfs(bigmatrix1),
  map = map_test

)

This works fine, however, when I'm trying to use that map_test in equijoin, it fails. So, when I try to run the following code (of course at the same session where I have run already those commands above):

test2 =
  equijoin (
  left.input = to.dfs(bigmatrix1),
  right.input = to.dfs(bigmatrix2),
  outer = "left",
  map.left =  map_test
,
    map.right =map_test
)

This fails and I get the following error message to the log

Error in keys(kv) : object 'map_test' not found Calls:  .. is.keyval -> map -> mark.side -> split.keyval -> keys Execution halted java.lang.RuntimeException: PipeMapRed.waitOutputThreads(): subprocess failed with code 1 at
...

However, if I run the same code where I just replace map_test with the function code, everything works fine

test2 =
  equijoin (
  left.input = to.dfs(bigmatrix1),
  right.input = to.dfs(bigmatrix2),
  outer = "left",
  map.left =   function(key, number_matrix){
         keys=number_matrix[,1]
         vals=number_matrix[,2:3]
       keyval(keys, vals)
     }

,
    map.right =  function(key, number_matrix){
         keys=number_matrix[,1]
         vals=number_matrix[,2:3]
       keyval(keys, vals)
     }

)

Why equijoin cannot "see" map_test from outside, while mapreduce can? I can of course use copy paste, but problem arises, if I'd like to use some variables defined outside the map.left and map.right functions, meaning that

This works:

cols=2:3

test1_1 =
  mapreduce (

  map = function(key, number_matrix){

         vals=number_matrix[,cols]
       keyval(keys, vals)

)

This doesn't

cols=2:3

test2_1 =
  equijoin (
  left.input = to.dfs(bigmatrix1),
  right.input = to.dfs(bigmatrix2),
  outer = "left",
  map.left =   function(key, number_matrix){

         keys=number_matrix[,1]
         vals=number_matrix[,cols]
       keyval(keys, vals)
     }

,
    map.right =  function(key, number_matrix){
         keys=number_matrix[,1]
         vals=number_matrix[,cols]
       keyval(keys, vals)
     }

)

(Error in map.right(k, v) : object 'cols' not found ) or (Error in map.left(k, v) : object 'cols' not found)

What I'm doing wrong?

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1004] RHadoop : Using custom input format
messages.body_plain:
Understand the problem now, thanks for the clarification. It may be a more than trivial issue with the design of from.dfs. In essence, when I wrote it I considered multiple files in the same directory as one data set and they get merged early in the process. The split into multiple files is not considered part of the data. Later on I realized that there are ways to process them separately in mapreduce, but these are not available in from.dfs. The problem is, are these part of the streaming specs of an artifact of how things are implemented? The other problem is who hard would it be to support this feature in from.dfs? I need to think about this.  For now one option is to add a field to the csv files with the name of the file or equivalent id, which will allow you to tell which record they come from. The other thing is that your usage may work in mapreduce because streaming supports it and that may be all that you need.

Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1004] RHadoop : Using custom input format
messages.body_plain:
I think before you spend more time down this road you should search for "Hadoop small file problem". There are many links, the classic is a Cloudera 2009 blog post but looking at this post http://amilaparanawithana.blogspot.com/2012/06/small-file-problem-in-hadoop.html it seems that as of 2012 the problem is still here. The message is, with files in the KB size, if you have enough of them to justify using Hadoop, it's not going to work. You should make each file a single record in a sequence file, for instance. This problem is not R or rmr specific, it's a Hadoop design choice. Since this is a characteristic of Hadoop, you can't use Hadoop to consolidate small files unless you are willing to pay the performance penalty, which is going to be severe according to reports available online, at least at the KB level. You need to look at the process that's creating the small files and change it. At least, that's what I would do from the limited information available.

Antonio

In essence, when I wrote it I considered multiple files in the same directory as one data set and they get merged early in the process. The split into multiple files is not considered part of the data. Later on I realized that there are ways to process them separately in mapreduce, but these are not available in from.dfs. The problem is, are these part of the streaming specs of an artifact of how things are implemented? The other problem is who hard would it be to support this feature in from.dfs? I need to think about this.  For now one option is to add a field to the csv files with the name of the file or equivalent id, which will allow you to tell which record they come from. sequence.typedbytes is a sequence file with a key and value both of type typedbyteswritable. I don't think we can read any sequence file as the mapping between any Java type and typedbytes is not defined.

Antonio

The message is, with files in the KB size, if you have enough of them to justify using Hadoop, it's not going to work. You should make each file a single record in a sequence file, for instance. This problem is not R or rmr specific, it's a Hadoop design choice. I can tell you what the difference is just to clarify it, but it should work either way and indeed it does in many instances. rmr2 saves two environments: the local environment inside the mapreduce call, which contains things like the map and reduce functions, and the global environment, which is not saved by the first call even if it is an enclosing environment for some of the objects therein. So when the map argument contains a global object, it needs to access the global env, which is saved separately. This is the difference between the copy and paste run and your preferred version (which I agree with you is the only one acceptable from a sw engineering point of view). Now to the difference between mapreduce and equijoin. Equijoin calls mapreduce with a map function that calls map.left and map.right. So there is one additional level of indirection. It seems that when this additional level of indirection is present, global environment objects become unavailable, as your second example confirms.

The message is, with files in the KB size, if you have enough of them to justify using Hadoop, it's not going to work. You should make each file a single record in a sequence file, for instance. This problem is not R or rmr specific, it's a Hadoop design choice. messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1020] Problem with equijoin map-functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
so that's a list of objects loaded to populate the global env. As you said, it isn't loading anything. The only rational explanation here is that you are installing slightly different versions of rmr2. At some point in development we tried a heuristic to decide which objects really needed to be saved and loaded on the nodes. It never worked so we removed it. Its limitations were exactly of the type you are seeing, that is if nesting is too deep, it would not detect needed objects. If you got your version from git and not from the downloads, it is possible that you are running with this heuristic still in. The different Hadoop mode is a red herring, there is no way Hadoop can affect this. The version with the broken heuristic was never released (unless something really bad happened). It was in the master branch briefly before being removed. The version number was already set to 2.3 in preparation for that release. My suggestion is to reinstall rmr2 on all the nodes where it is failing getting the "official" 2.3 download, and see if that fixes it. It would be  nice to have a hash of the source automatically generated to track even the smallest change of the source, but I am not sure how I could automate that, suggestions are welcome. Then rmr2 at load time would put this hash in stderr helping users keep all installs consistent.

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
Hi Antonio,

 thank you very much for your help. I found that parameter on my client configuration files and was set to 1 :-(

 I changed it to a higher value and all my problems went away.

 You were 100% right about my test file :-O short lines with vocabulary huge and uniformly distributed.
 I do this performance tests with wordcount because I'm also comparing against a Java's wordcount. I'm comparing also the performance depending on the file size.

 Now I want to get better performance because there's too much difference between R and Java. I see that Revolution Analytics have rmr, rhdfs and rhbase, are they the same versions that you have on GitHub? I wonder if they have just optimized R or also your libraries.

Best regards,
 Jorge

On Tuesday, October 1, 2013 6:44:58 PM UTC+2, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:
> First keep in mind examples are in general not optimizes but kept as simple as possible.
>
> The number of reduce tasks defaults to one in many Hadoop distribution. You need to change that. One way is to supply this additional argument to mapreduce
>
> backend.parameters = list(hadoop= list(D = "mapred.reduce.tasks=10"))
>
>
> where 10 should be actually slightly less than the number of available reduce slots. This argument is deprecated because it was being abused, but I think this use case will be preserved by whatever replaces it. The memory issue points to something else, like a word with a very large count. Even then, with the combiner on, it should work. Nonetheless I would check that the pattern is appropriate for your file, that would be single space separated words. Another thing is to try with a smaller, local file, say 1 mb, on the local backend, do a debug(wc.map) and debug(wc.reduce) and see that it is doing what you expect it to do. Have you tried different data sizes and wrote down the different times-to-completion for the map phase and reduce pahse? How do they grow? That usually gives some insight.  Another thing you can do is adding
>
> rmr.str(word)
> rmr.str(counts)
>
> as the first two lines of the reduce function. It will write a lot in your std error, so use at smaller data sizes.

I managed to get within 20% of Java on a collocation analysis task. That was on EC2 were some of the network latencies and other overhead may mask the differences. On a smaller dataset on my laptop the difference was 6X, with the R implementation constantly CPU-bound. If you don't bring in other dimensions in your analysis, such as the productivity and greater statistical sophistication afforded by R, I can spare you the effort, just go with Java. Then please complain on linkedin you can't find enough data scientists! The wordcount example is what it is, an example for purpose of explanation and teaching and there may be optimizations available that I haven't thought of. If you want you can turn the profile.nodes option on and share the data produced with me and I will take a look. I would also try to increase the keyval.length option 10X and see if that helps.

The Revolution distribution is behind github by a few versions. RHadoop will run on Revo R and take advantage of the optimizations therein, nonetheless I would advise against running RevoR in multicore mode on Hadoop as having two separate mechanism for parallelism will probably create problems more than solve them.

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
sessionInfo will only tell you if functional is loaded, hence installed, locally. We need to make sure it's available on the nodes as well. rmr2 has a dependency on functional, if you call that a problem maybe you shouldn't be using rmr2. But it shouldn't be impossible to fix. If you haven't installed all of the rmr2 dependencies on the nodes, please do so. If you have but they don't seem to be available, please install them under a system path were they are going to be available to all users. While installation under a custom directory should be possible, we found that users have trouble pulling that one off for reasons that aren't totally clear. I hope this helps

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
So far as I could tell, my installation process went smoothly and correctly, but perhaps my environment variables are wrong, because as soon as I entered the first line of  a sample program I got the error listed below.

I used Centos 6.4 and yum. I installed Cloudera Hadoop 4 and R 3.0.1, and also I installed rmr2, quickcheck, and the rmr2 dependencies.

I exported environment variables as follows:
HADOOP_CMD=/usr/bin/hadoop
HADOOP_STREAMING=/usr/lib/hadoop-mapreduce

I chose the streaming directory because I assumed that it should contain a jar with the word "streaming," and that is the only directory I found with jars that match.  In particular:
# ls /usr/lib/hadoop-mapreduce/ | grep streaming
hadoop-streaming-2.0.0-cdh4.4.0.jar
hadoop-streaming.jar

I tried the program at:
https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/rmr2/blob/master/docs/tutorial.md

However, I know that the HADOOP_STREAMING directory should contain a jar with "streaming" in its name, and /usr/lib/hadoop does not contain any .jar with "streaming."

> library(rmr2)
Loading required package: Rcpp
Loading required package: RJSONIO
Loading required package: bitops
Loading required package: digest
Loading required package: functional
Loading required package: stringr

> small.ints = to.dfs(1:1000)

Instead use the hdfs command for it.

Exception in thread "main" java.io.IOException: Error opening job jar: /usr/lib/hadoop-mapreduce

    at java.util.zip.ZipFile.<init>(ZipFile.java:132)
    at java.util.jar.JarFile.<init>(JarFile.java:151)

>

I am not sure that the problem is my variables;  possibly I need to downgrade R from 3.0.1 to 2.15, or perhaps I need to change something else.

Thanks.

>From the Wiki (https://github.com/RevolutionAnalytics/RHadoop/wiki/rhbase),  The install steps for thrift are:

Install all Thrift pre-requisites: http://wiki.apache.org/thrift/GettingCentOS5Packages
Build Thrfit according to instructions: http://wiki.apache.org/thrift/ThriftInstallation
Update PKG_CONFIG_PATH:export PKG_CONFIG_PATH=$PKG_CONFIG_PATH:/usr/local/lib/pkgconfig/
Verifiy pkg-config path is correct: pkg-config --cflags thrift , returns:-I/usr/local/include/thrift
Copy Thrift library sudo cp /usr/local/lib/libthrift-0.8.0.so <http://libthrift-0.8.0.so> /usr/lib/

Did you complete steps 3,4 and 5?

First question: Is anyone in this group currently successfully using rhbase with Cloudera Hadoop?

Second question: My understanding is that the preferred method is just to type <hbase thrift start> at the console, then type<R> and enter the R environment, at which point one should be able to use commands like <library(rhbase)> and <hb.init()>.  Is this the correct way to use rhbase?

Third question: I have noted that previous people who have asked about zookeeper have been directed to ask Cloudera.  I guess this means that no one in this discussion group currently requires zookeeper to use hbase. Is that correct?

Thanks

I set up Hadoop 1.2.1 in pseudo-distributed mode.

I used the standard settings for the core-site.xml, namely:
 <value>hdfs://localhost:9000</value>
I verified that ssh worked and ran the example jobs correctly with plain Hadoop.
I verified that R had everything necessary for rmr2 and rhdfs.

HADOOP_CMD=/home/user/hadoop-1.2.1/bin/hadoop

> hdfs.init()
13/10/23 15:22:12 INFO ipc.Client: Retrying connect to server: localhost/127.0.0.1:9000 <http://127.0.0.1:9000>. Already tried 0 time(s); retry policy is RetryUpToMaximumCountWithFixedSleep(maxRetries=10, sleepTime=1 SECONDS)

  java.net.ConnectException: Call to localhost/127.0.0.1:9000 <http://127.0.0.1:9000> failed on connection exception: java.net.ConnectException: Connection refused

I looked at some webpages from people who had gotten similar errors and tried some tactics that had worked for them.

Some people had success from modifyi        <property>
                <name>dfs.permissions</name>

I imitated the above measures but continued to have connection problems.

messages.subject: Re: rhdfs can't use hdfs.init()
messages.body_plain:
Fixed!

I had been following suggestions from old tutorials about pseudo-distributed mode.  These old tutorials did not use complicated versions of the .xml files.

However, when the .xml files are easy, for some reason, the namenode shuts down with the following errors in the logs:

2013-10-24 10:09:46,734 INFO org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.common.Storage: Storage directory /tmp/hadoop-user/dfs/name does not exist
2013-10-24 10:09:46,736 ERROR org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSNamesystem: FSNamesystem initialization failed.
org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.common.InconsistentFSStateException: Directory /tmp/hadoop-user/dfs/name is in an inconsistent state: storage directory does not exist or is not accessible.
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSImage.recoverTransitionRead(FSImage.java:304)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSDirectory.loadFSImage(FSDirectory.java:104)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSNamesystem.initialize(FSNamesystem.java:427)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSNamesystem.<init>(FSNamesystem.java:395)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.initialize(NameNode.java:299)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.<init>(NameNode.java:569)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.createNameNode(NameNode.java:1479)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.main(NameNode.java:1488)
2013-10-24 10:09:46,744 ERROR org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode: org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.common.InconsistentFSStateException: Directory /tmp/hadoop-user/dfs/name is in an inconsistent state: storage directory does not exist or is not accessible.
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSImage.recoverTransitionRead(FSImage.java:304)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSDirectory.loadFSImage(FSDirectory.java:104)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSNamesystem.initialize(FSNamesystem.java:427)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.FSNamesystem.<init>(FSNamesystem.java:395)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.initialize(NameNode.java:299)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.<init>(NameNode.java:569)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.createNameNode(NameNode.java:1479)
        at org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode.main(NameNode.java:1488)

2013-10-24 10:09:46,745 INFO org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.namenode.NameNode: SHUTDOWN_MSG:

. . .
The good news is that the .xml files can be fixed to prevent this namenode shutdown.

In particular, I modded hdfs-site.xml to include:

 <property>
  <name>dfs.name.dir</name>
  <value>/home/user/bigdataname</value>
 </property>
<property>
   <name>dfs.data.dir</name>
   <value>/home/user/hadoopdata</value>
</property>

and as a result, basic mapreduce works within R with to.dfs and from.dfs

m<-from.dfs(xbar)

diffsquare=mapreduce(input="/user/test/test2.txt", map = function(k,v) { keyval(1,sum(as.numeric(v)-as.numeric(m$val))^2 )},reduce = function(k,v) {keyval(1,sum(as.numeric(v)) )} )

messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#1088] Re: How to find variance in RHadoop?
messages.body_plain:
Since the chunks of data that are passed to the map function in the map phase, by taking the mean of arbitrary subsets of the data you put yourself in a dead end. What do you do with a collection of means? I would say, just compute the same and the sum of squares and a count of data points. Then the variance is E[X^2] - E[X]^2. Let me know if this gets you going.

Antonio

For finding out E(X^2), I used the following map/reduce functions

map = function(k,v) { keyval(1,(as.numeric(v))^2)}
reduce = function(k,v) {keyval(length(v),sum(v)/length(v))}

map1 =    function(k,v) { keyval(1,as.numeric(v))}
reduce1 = function(k,v) {keyval(length(v),(sum(v)/length(v))^2)}

In both the instances, since map function emits only one key of value 1, the
load will be only on one reducer. Only one reducer will be summing up all numbers.

Hi I am trying to gain some inside on how to get the best performance out of R.

The task is to process large datasets and change writings of strings (e.g. small letters to capital letters) and extract parts of strings, so far done via regular expressions.

My question now is, how can I work with large data sets, up to 1TB. So far I glanced at the big memory package but more promising to me seems to be the Rhadoop package. I wonder if it can handle the tasks I described above. I couldn't find any solid information on all the capabilities of the Rhadoop/rmr package.

Any ideas or new insight are greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#1108] Re: General question
messages.body_plain:
I don't think this is the intended use case, but this is a general Hadoop question and I am sure you can find more information about it. There is plenty of tutorials of how to get a single node Hadoop cluster going, for instance

http://www.michael-noll.com/tutorials/running-hadoop-on-ubuntu-linux-single-node-cluster/

or

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/3406839/running-a-standalone-hadoop-application-on-multiple-cpu-cores

It's not clear to me if you'd be better off running in distributed or pseudo-distributed mode. You may have to ask on Hadoop forums for better answers.

And you can easily try one of the VMs available, like Hortonworks' sandbox, which is really an easy process, but I wonder if you are going to get the performance you want out of it. Hadoop's strength is scalability to large systems, not performance on small systems, and on a single node you may be willing to consider other options, like the package foreach. On the other hand, if your setup is expected to get larger, with more data and more machines, maybe it is the smart thing to develop code once and for all, ready for the larger scale. rmr2 will do whatever hadoop does: it's pretty much unaware of Hadoop's configuration.

Antonio
